zh.summary: 從生活與虛構教材平台案例，分辨釣魚、魚叉式釣魚與鯨釣，練習可信管道驗證與證據判讀。

sourceBody.text: CEH M09-02｜釣魚、魚叉式釣魚與鯨釣
Module 09：Social Engineering（社交工程） 路線原名：Phishing、Spear Phishing、Whaling 建議閱讀時間：10～12 分鐘。
一、先說結論：先看「鎖定誰」，再看「要你做什麼」
昨天談到，社交工程會利用人的信任，讓人替對方打開原本不該開的門。今天把其中一種常見手法看清楚：釣魚。
先想像你經營一家咖啡廳。有人傳訊息說：「你的店家帳號有問題，請從這裡重新登入。」
這段話不一定是真的系統通知，也可能是有人假裝成平台客服，想讓你把密碼輸入他的假網站。
如果他把一樣的話傳給很多店家，是常見的廣撒網釣魚；如果他知道你的姓名、店名及剛參加的活動，專門替你設計內容，就是更有針對性的釣魚；如果他專挑能核准大筆款項的負責人下手，就是今天要認識的鯨釣。
重點不是背三個英文單字，而是學會判斷：對方鎖定誰？利用什麼背景讓人相信？想誘導什麼行動？
二、三個名詞怎麼分？
1. Phishing（釣魚）：用看似可信的訊息，引你做出不安全的行動
Phishing 可以想成「放一個看起來可信的餌，讓人自己上鉤」。在資訊安全裡，常見情況是冒充可信的人或機構，誘使你透露帳號密碼、敏感資料，或前往假的網站。它是數位社交工程的一種。[NIST：Phishing](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)
例如，「包裹資料待補」「帳號即將停用」「檔案需要重新登入才能開啟」，都可以被拿來當理由。這些理由本身不等於詐騙；關鍵是訊息是否具有欺騙性，以及它要你做的事是否經過驗證。
也不要把釣魚只想成騙密碼。誘導開啟惡意附件、交出資料或轉帳，都可能是目標。
廣撒網很常見，但「大量寄送」不是釣魚的必要條件。 Phishing 是上位概念，下面兩種仍屬於釣魚。
2. Spear Phishing（魚叉式釣魚／定向釣魚）：內容特別針對某個對象
Spear 是魚叉。撒網是碰碰運氣，魚叉則是先瞄準目標。
魚叉式釣魚會針對特定個人、團隊或組織，利用與對方有關的背景，讓訊息看起來更像真的。例如，訊息提到你正在處理的專案，還用你平常合作對象的名字。
判斷重點是「有針對性的內容與目標」，不是一定只寄給一個人，也不是一定寫出全名。
3. Whaling（鯨釣）：專門瞄準高階、高價值目標
Whale 是鯨魚，這裡用來比喻具有較大決策權、資金權限或敏感資訊存取權的高階目標，例如執行長、董事長或高階主管。
鯨釣通常可以理解為魚叉式釣魚中，專門針對這些高階對象的一種。不是訊息提到大筆金額，就自動叫鯨釣；要看被鎖定的受害對象。
加拿大資安中心區分：魚叉式釣魚可針對個人、群體或組織；鯨釣則鎖定高知名度人士或高階主管。[加拿大資安中心：辨認惡意電子郵件](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/spotting-malicious-email-messages-itsap00100)

rows: 用欺騙性訊息引導不安全的行動
定向釣魚的目標是高階、高價值人物

sourceBody.text: 三者不是互不相干的三個盒子：鯨釣也是定向釣魚，也屬於釣魚。 考題若同時出現幾種答案，要看題幹是否提供足夠線索，選擇最貼切的分類。
三、一個完整例子：同一家教材平台，三種不同的「餌」
以下全部是虛構的 Northstar 教材平台情境，不涉及真實對象，也不需要寄送或測試任何訊息。
Northstar 使用雲端服務保存教材、學員資料與公司文件。
情境 A：很多人收到同一份帳號通知
多名員工收到沒有個人背景的訊息，要求從陌生連結登入，否則帳號會停用。後續查證發現那是假登入頁。
這是典型的 Phishing。它借用大家對「帳號不能出問題」的擔心，誘導交出登入資料。
情境 B：只針對教材專案承辦人的合作通知
承辦人小林收到一封訊息，提到他正在處理的教材專案與合作單位，要求登入查看「修訂附件」。後續確認，合作單位沒有寄出這項要求。
這是 Spear Phishing：有特定對象，也有量身設計的背景。
知道專案名稱可能讓人比較相信，但那些資訊也可能來自公開活動、社群貼文或先前外流資料。知道事情，不代表具有身分或授權。
情境 C：專門給執行長的董事會文件通知
攻擊者鎖定執行長，以公司近期董事會議題為背景，誘導他透過假的入口查看機密文件。
這是 Whaling。分類關鍵在於執行長是被鎖定的高階目標，而不只是郵件寫得正式。
最容易考錯的一點：假冒主管，不一定就是鯨釣
如果攻擊者假冒執行長，實際去騙一般承辦人，不能只因為寄件者顯示「執行長」就判定是鯨釣。
要分清楚：

items: 冒充誰：用哪個身分增加可信感。
攻擊誰：希望哪個收件者上當。

sourceBody.text: 這是從前面的定義推導出的判斷方式。資訊不足時，可以先判斷為疑似定向釣魚，不必硬貼上更細的標籤。
四、它為什麼有用？把「看起來合理」接到「危險動作」
從防守者的角度，可以用下面的理解流程整理；這是本課的教學整理，不是官方固定攻擊階段：
熟悉的身分或背景 → 看似合理的理由 → 要求你採取行動 → 行動跨過安全界線 → 可能造成損害。
用小林的情境來看：

rows: 熟悉的合作單位與教材名稱
是否獨立確認過寄件來源？
這是否符合原本工作流程？
為什麼不能從原本的正式入口查看？
登入資料交給未核實網站
這個地方是否真的有權接收資料？
帳號遭冒用、教材或學員資料被存取
有哪些實際紀錄能確認影響？

sourceBody.text: 這也接回 M01-02：資產是帳號與資料；威脅是誘導揭露或冒用；弱點可能是缺少驗證的工作流程；風險則還要看成功可能性與後果。
不是收到訊息就代表入侵成功。 中間每一步都需要自己的證據。
五、不要只靠錯字、Logo 或熟悉語氣判斷
錯字多、要求很急、寄件網址不對，確實值得警覺；但沒有這些警訊，不代表安全。
尤其 AI（人工智慧） 可以協助產生流暢文字、整理公開背景資訊，讓釣魚內容更像真實往來。社群平台上的假客服或冒充帳號，也可能是入口，不只電子郵件才有釣魚。[加拿大資安中心：認識與避免釣魚攻擊](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks)
因此，下面幾句推論都不夠：

items: 「沒有錯字，所以是真的。」
「對方知道我在做什麼，所以一定是本人。」
「頭像與名稱一樣，所以帳號沒問題。」
「他叫我再問這個客服，所以有查證過了。」

sourceBody.text: 最後一點尤其重要：如果查證電話、客服帳號或網站也是可疑訊息提供的，你可能只是換一個地方，繼續跟同一個攻擊者確認。
本課先掌握文字訊息的判斷。電話、簡訊與身分冒充，會在下一單元接著學；聲音或影像看起來像本人，也不能讓驗證流程消失。
六、防護怎麼做？先停止危險動作，再用既有可信管道確認
不是要求你永遠不開信，而是遇到涉及登入、資料、金錢或權限的要求時，補上必要查核。
個人當下可以做的事

items: 1. 先不要照可疑訊息操作。 不急著登入、開附件、提供驗證碼或交出資料。
2. 改從已知可信的入口處理。 例如自己原先保存的正式服務入口，而不是訊息裡新給的入口。
3. 使用既有聯絡方式核實。 從公司原本的通訊錄聯絡合作窗口，確認「是否真的有這個要求、對哪些資料、要做到什麼程度」。
4. 依組織流程通報。 保留可疑訊息交給指定的資訊或資安窗口，不散發給其他同事試點。

sourceBody.text: 加拿大資安中心也建議，對可疑要求使用其他管道確認，而不是直接跟著郵件內的連結或附件走。[辨認惡意電子郵件](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/spotting-malicious-email-messages-itsap00100)
組織不能只要求員工「小心一點」
在 Northstar 這個教學案例，可以設計：

items: 重要資料只透過既有平台交付，減少臨時改用陌生入口。
付款對象、收款資料或權限變更，有獨立核准程序。
員工能快速通報，而且通報錯誤不被責怪，避免有人因害怕挨罵而隱瞞。
限制帳號權限，避免一個帳號出問題就能取得所有資料。
保留必要的登入與資料存取紀錄，方便查清楚實際影響。

sourceBody.text: 這些是本例的防守設計，不是每個組織都適用的固定清單。具體做法要符合自己的系統與授權範圍。
七、防護與證據判讀：不要把「看到」「點過」「被入侵」混成一件事
小林說：「我好像點過那個連結。」這是需要立即處理的線索，但還不是完整的事件結論。

rows: 有互動的陳述，待紀錄比對
應視為可能的憑證暴露並處置
攻擊者一定已成功登入
有可疑的成功登入紀錄
需要確認登入者與相關活動
有資料下載或外傳跡象
需查範圍、內容、時間與接收方
未被記錄的所有情況都已釐清

sourceBody.text: 可以把調查分成三層：

items: 觀察：郵件內容、使用者陳述、系統紀錄實際顯示什麼。
推論：這些線索可能代表什麼。
驗證：透過授權取得的紀錄交叉確認，排除其他合理解釋。

sourceBody.text: 例如「異常登入」也可能是本人換了裝置，不能單憑一項警示就定案；反過來，沒有找到紀錄，也不代表一定沒發生，因為紀錄可能不完整。
如果已經輸入密碼或執行可疑檔案，不要為了查清楚而再次打開它。應立即向負責窗口說明做過哪些動作，依既有事件應變流程處理帳號與裝置；不要自行刪除所有痕跡。蒐集與測試只限合法授權範圍。
八、今天先記住四句話

items: 1. Phishing： 用欺騙性訊息引你做不安全的事。
2. Spear Phishing： 針對特定對象設計內容，不一定只有一位收件者。
3. Whaling： 定向釣魚鎖定高階、高價值人物；不要只看冒充的是誰。
4. 防守關鍵： 信任不能取代驗證；收到訊息也不等於攻擊成功。

sourceBody.text: 九、小檢核：你會怎麼判斷？
虛構的 Northstar 一位一般財務承辦人收到訊息。寄件者顯示為執行長，信中正確提到近期教材專案，要求把合作款項改匯到新帳戶，並強調「先不要打電話，我正在開會」。目前只知道承辦人收到訊息，尚未確認是否照做。
A. 如果查證確認這是攻擊，最貼切的分類是一般釣魚、魚叉式釣魚，還是可以直接斷定為鯨釣？理由是什麼？
B. 對方知道專案名稱，能不能證明這項要求是真的？下一步應該怎麼確認？
C. 現在能不能直接寫「公司已被騙款」？還缺哪些證據？
先試著用自己的話回答，不需要背課本文字。參考答案供自我對照，不代表已經完成作答或理解驗證。

paragraphs: 小檢核參考解答
A：優先判斷為魚叉式釣魚，不因冒充執行長就直接叫鯨釣
訊息鎖定特定承辦人，還使用教材專案背景來增加可信度，因此符合有針對性的魚叉式釣魚。它也屬於廣義的釣魚。
鯨釣要看被鎖定的高階目標，不是只看冒充的身分。本題真正被騙的目標是一般財務承辦人，所以不能只因寄件者顯示為執行長，就直接判成鯨釣。若新增其他證據，分類仍可再評估。
B：知道背景不等於取得授權，要換到既有可信的管道
專案資料可能來自公開資訊、外流內容或被冒用的帳號。應先停止變更匯款資料，使用原本公司通訊錄或其他已核實的聯絡方式，確認這個具體要求，並走既有的付款變更與核准流程。
不要使用這封信新提供的電話、連結或客服帳號來「證明這封信是真的」，也不要因對方說正在開會，就跳過必要程序。
C：還不能說已經被騙款
目前只證實收到訊息。還要釐清承辦人是否回覆、是否變更帳戶、是否提出或核准付款，以及實際付款紀錄。也需要確認收款對象與款項狀態。不能把付款申請當成已付款，也不能把收到釣魚信當成已受害。
適當的初步紀錄可以是：「收到疑似定向釣魚訊息；是否變更付款資料、是否實際付款，仍待確認。」若情境後續已證實為攻擊，可更新攻擊判定，但款項影響仍須各自查核。

en.summary: Distinguish phishing, spear phishing and whaling through everyday and fictional examples, independent verification and evidence-based judgment.

sourceBody.text: CEH M09-02 | Phishing, Spear Phishing, and Whaling
Module 09: Social Engineering Route title: Phishing, Spear Phishing, Whaling Suggested reading time: 10–12 minutes.
1. The conclusion first: look at who is targeted, then what you are asked to do
In the previous lesson, we saw how social engineering exploits trust to persuade someone to open a door that should remain closed. Today we examine one common approach: phishing.
Imagine you run a café. Someone sends a message saying, “There is a problem with your business account. Sign in again here.”
It might not be a real system notification. Someone could be pretending to be platform support, hoping you will enter your password on their fake website.

Sending the same message to many businesses is a common broad phishing approach. Knowing your name, café name, and a recent event you attended, then tailoring a message to you, makes the attempt more targeted. Deliberately pursuing the senior decision-maker who can approve substantial payments introduces whaling.
The goal is not simply to memorize three terms. Ask: who is being targeted, what background makes the message believable, and what action does it try to induce?
2. How do the three terms differ?
Phishing: using apparently trustworthy communication to induce unsafe action

Think of phishing as setting convincing bait and waiting for someone to take it. In information security, a common pattern is impersonating a trusted person or organization to obtain credentials or sensitive information, or direct someone to a fake website. It is a form of digital social engineering. [NIST: Phishing](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)

“Missing delivery information,” “your account will be disabled,” and “sign in again to open this document” can all serve as pretexts. Those subjects do not themselves prove fraud. What matters is whether the communication is deceptive and whether the requested action has been verified.
Phishing is not limited to stealing passwords. Opening a malicious attachment, disclosing information, or transferring money can also be the intended outcome.
Mass distribution is common, but it is not a requirement. Phishing is the broader concept; the following two types are still phishing.
Spear phishing: tailoring the approach to a particular target
A fishing net catches whatever comes along; a spear is aimed first.

Spear phishing targets a particular person, team, or organization and uses relevant background to make the communication seem authentic. A message might mention your current project and use the name of a familiar partner.
The defining feature is a targeted audience and tailored approach—not necessarily one recipient or the use of a full name.
Whaling: pursuing senior, high-value targets

The whale represents a high-level target with substantial decision-making authority, financial authority, or access to sensitive information, such as a chief executive, chairperson, or senior manager.

Whaling can generally be understood as spear phishing specifically directed at such targets. Mentioning a large amount of money does not automatically make a message whaling. Look at the intended victim.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security distinguishes spear phishing directed at individuals, groups, or organizations from whaling directed at high-profile individuals or senior executives. [Spotting malicious email messages](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/spotting-malicious-email-messages-itsap00100)

rows: Content is designed for particular targets
A targeted attack pursues a senior, high-value person

sourceBody.text: These are not three unrelated boxes: whaling is also targeted phishing and belongs to the broader phishing category. If an exam offers several of these answers, use the evidence in the question to select the most specific appropriate classification.
3. One connected example: three kinds of bait at the same learning platform
The following Northstar learning-platform scenarios are fictional. They involve no real targets and require no messages or tests to be sent.
Northstar uses cloud services to store learning materials, student information, and company documents.
Scenario A: many employees receive the same account notification

Several employees receive a generic message asking them to sign in through an unfamiliar link or lose access to their accounts. Subsequent investigation establishes that the destination is a fake login page.
This is typical phishing. It uses concern about losing account access to obtain login information.
Scenario B: a collaboration notice tailored to the project coordinator

Lin, a project coordinator, receives a message mentioning the learning-material project and its partner organization. It asks Lin to sign in to view a “revised attachment.” The partner subsequently confirms it did not send that request.
This is spear phishing: a particular target and tailored context.

Knowing the project name may make the message convincing, but that information could come from a public event, social-media post, or previous data exposure. Knowing facts does not establish identity or authorization.
Scenario C: a board-document notice designed for the chief executive
An attacker targets the chief executive and uses recent board business as the context for a fake document-access portal.
This is whaling. The defining feature is the senior executive being targeted, not simply a formal writing style.
A common exam mistake: impersonating an executive does not automatically mean whaling
If an attacker pretends to be the chief executive but actually targets an ordinary coordinator, the sender name “CEO” does not by itself justify a whaling classification.
Separate:

items: Who is impersonated: the identity used to appear credible.
Who is targeted: the recipient the attacker wants to deceive.

sourceBody.text: This distinction follows from the definitions above. If information is incomplete, identify suspected targeted phishing without forcing a more specific label.
4. Why does it work? Connecting a plausible story to a dangerous action
From a defender’s perspective, the following sequence helps organize the situation. It is a teaching aid, not an official fixed set of attack phases:
Familiar identity or context → plausible reason → requested action → a security boundary is crossed → possible harm.
Apply this to Lin’s scenario:

rows: A familiar partner and project name
Has the source been independently verified?
Does this fit the established workflow?
Sign in through the message link
Why not use the existing official portal?
Credentials go to an unverified site
Is that destination authorized to receive them?
Account misuse or access to materials and student data
What records establish the actual impact?

sourceBody.text: This reconnects to M01-02: accounts and information are assets; deceptive disclosure or impersonation is a threat; an unverified workflow may be a weakness; risk still depends on likelihood and consequences.
Receiving the message does not mean an intrusion succeeded. Every intermediate step needs its own evidence.
5. Do not rely only on spelling, logos, or a familiar tone
Misspellings, urgency, and incorrect sender domains are warning signs. Their absence does not establish safety.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can help produce fluent text and organize public background information, making phishing messages resemble genuine correspondence. Fake support accounts and impersonation on social platforms can also provide entry points; phishing is not limited to email. [Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: Recognize and avoid phishing attacks](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks)
These conclusions are therefore insufficient:

items: “There are no typos, so it is genuine.”
“They know what I am working on, so it must be the real person.”
“The picture and display name match, so the account is trustworthy.”
“They told me to ask this support contact, so I verified it.”

sourceBody.text: The last point is particularly important: if the verification phone number, support account, or website came from the suspicious message, you may simply be asking the same attacker through another interface.
This lesson focuses on written messages. Voice, text-message attacks, and impersonation are developed in the next unit. A convincing voice or image does not eliminate the need for verification.
6. Defending yourself: stop the risky action and verify through a known channel
You do not need to refuse all email. You need appropriate checks when a request concerns authentication, information, money, or permissions.
What an individual can do immediately

items: 1. Do not follow the suspicious request yet. Avoid rushing to sign in, open an attachment, disclose a verification code, or send information.
2. Use an already trusted entry point. For example, use the official service address you previously saved instead of a newly supplied link.
3. Verify through an established contact method. Use the organization’s existing directory to contact the partner and confirm the specific request, information involved, and intended scope.
4. Report through the organization’s process. Preserve the suspicious message for the designated IT or security contact rather than circulating it for colleagues to test.

sourceBody.text: The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security likewise recommends confirming suspicious requests through another means rather than following embedded links or attachments. [Spotting malicious email messages](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/spotting-malicious-email-messages-itsap00100)
Organizations need more than “be careful”
For the fictional Northstar organization, possible defensive designs include:

items: Deliver important information through established portals, reducing unexpected switches to unfamiliar ones.
Require independent approval for changes to payees, payment details, or access rights.
Provide quick, blame-free reporting so people do not hide mistakes out of fear.
Limit account permissions so one compromised account cannot access everything.
Retain appropriate login and information-access records to establish actual impact.

sourceBody.text: These are defensive design choices for this example, not a universal checklist. Implementation must fit the organization’s systems and authorization boundaries.
7. Evidence: receiving, clicking, and being compromised are different things
Lin says, “I think I clicked the link.” That is a lead requiring prompt attention, not a complete incident finding.

rows: The user reports clicking a link
A reported interaction, pending comparison with records
The user reports entering a password
The attacker definitely logged in successfully
A suspicious successful login is recorded
The identity and related activity need checking
Scope, content, timing, and recipient need investigation
Every unrecorded possibility has been resolved

sourceBody.text: Separate three layers:

items: Observation: what the message, user statement, or system record actually shows.
Inference: what those indicators may mean.
Verification: corroborating authorized records and considering other reasonable explanations.

sourceBody.text: For example, an unusual login may be the legitimate user on a new device; a single alert is not a complete finding. Conversely, missing records do not prove nothing happened, because logging may be incomplete.

If credentials were entered or a suspicious file was executed, do not reopen it just to investigate. Promptly tell the responsible team exactly what actions occurred and follow the established incident-response process for the account and device. Do not independently erase all traces. Evidence collection and testing must remain within legitimate authorization.
8. Four sentences to remember

items: 1. Phishing: deceptive communication tries to induce unsafe action.
2. Spear phishing: content targets particular recipients; there may be more than one.
3. Whaling: targeted phishing pursues senior, high-value people; do not classify only by the impersonated identity.
4. Defensive principle: trust does not replace verification, and receiving a message does not prove a successful attack.

sourceBody.text: 9. Quick check: how would you assess this?

An ordinary finance coordinator at fictional Northstar receives a message displaying the chief executive’s name. It correctly mentions a recent learning-material project, asks for a partner payment to be redirected to a new account, and says, “Do not call first; I am in a meeting.” So far, only receipt of the message is established; whether the coordinator acted on it is unknown.
A. If investigation confirms an attack, is the best description general phishing, spear phishing, or definitely whaling? Why?
B. Does knowing the project name prove the request is genuine? How should it be verified?
C. Can the incident already be recorded as “the company was defrauded of money”? What evidence is still missing?

Try answering in your own words rather than memorizing a definition. Reference answers support self-checking; their publication does not establish that you have answered or demonstrated understanding.

paragraphs: Reference answers
A: Prefer spear phishing; impersonating the chief executive does not by itself make it whaling
The message targets a particular coordinator and uses project-specific background to appear credible. That supports a spear-phishing classification. It also belongs to the broader phishing category.

Whaling is identified by the senior target, not only the impersonated identity. The intended victim here is an ordinary finance coordinator, so a CEO display name alone does not establish whaling. Additional evidence could justify revisiting the classification.
B: Knowing background information is not authorization; use an established trusted channel

Project information might come from public sources, exposed data, or a misused account. Stop the payment-detail change, use the existing company directory or another previously verified contact method to confirm this particular request, and follow the established change-approval process.

Do not use a new phone number, link, or support account supplied by this message to “prove the message is genuine.” A claim that the sender is in a meeting does not justify bypassing the required procedure.
C: A financial loss is not established yet

Only receipt is confirmed. Determine whether the coordinator replied, changed account details, requested or approved payment, and what the actual payment records show. Verify the recipient and payment status. A payment request is not a completed payment, and receiving phishing is not the same as suffering the intended harm.

An appropriate initial record might say: “Suspected targeted phishing received; changes to payment details and actual payment remain unconfirmed.” If the attack is later confirmed, update that finding while continuing to verify financial impact separately.
